Reflecting on my meeting with Dr. Karl, I now realize it impacted me far more deeply than teaching me one piece of trivia about the Chinese military. For you see, Dr. Karl is famous for (among other things) his research on belly button lint. And over 20 years after meeting him, unconsciously inspired by his work no doubt, I started collecting my own belly button lint.. like the well-adjusted citizen that I am.

I have been at it for 5 years now.. in fact, it’s the poster-child displayed on the Wikipedia entry for navel lint. I may not have walked away with all the answers that day, but years later I salvaged something far more valuable:

1

Today I learned Dr. Karl’s full name is Karl Sven Woytek Sas Konkovitch Matthew Kruszelnicki, which is excellent. I wish my middle name was Konkovitch, instead of being stuck with Glen (sorry Glenn)

2

This reddit thread shows people boasting about having photographic memory like how I (and I think most people) understand it to work.

3

Well.. I guess he’s boasted about it a little bit. Okay.. maybe a lot.

4

i.e. You need to be good at deciding what information to trust and aggregating evidence to decide what’s true

5

When digging into this, I came across the alleged cases of Solomon Shereshevsky and "Elizabeth" (who doesn’t get a last name for some reason):

Solomon was studied extensively by neuropsychologist Alexander Luria in the 1920s. He could allegedly recall long lists of numbers, words, and nonsense syllables years after being exposed to them once. His extraordinary memory didn't come from a photographic ability but rather from an unusual form of synesthesia – information triggered multiple sensory experiences for him. Numbers weren't just visual symbols; they had colors, textures, and tastes. Does this count? I’m not sure. Meanwhile, despite his remarkable memory abilities, Shereshevsky struggled in many aspects of life. He had difficulty understanding abstract concepts and metaphors. His memory was almost too detailed, preventing him from seeing the forest for the trees. Far from ruling the world, he worked as a reporter and later as a professional mnemonist performing memory feats.

Elizabeth was a Harvard student who, in 1970, became the subject of research when she claimed to be able to recall poetry written in a foreign language that she didn't understand years after seeing it, and being able to recall random dot patterns with perfect precision. Elizabeth remains the only person documented to have passed such a test. However, there are serious questions about this research. The methods used in the testing procedures have been criticized, particularly given the extraordinary nature of the claims. Adding to the skepticism is the fact that Stromeyer married his subject, and Elizabeth has consistently refused to repeat the tests. No one has ever replicated these results.

item.title: "You wouldn't download a car!"
item.description: ..because you couldn't. But if you could, I reckon it'd be totally fine!
item.content:encoded:
Back in 2015, I wrote down my argument that intellectual property rights are largely bogus. Ten years later, I’m still pirating content1, but I sometimes feel guilty about it. So I figured it was time to revisit my old arguments and see if they hold up.

Are copyright and patent protections actually necessary/beneficial? Or are they unjustified philosophically, and have net negative outcomes in practice..

The majority of this post will be a polished up version of my notes from a decade ago. After all, why write something new when I can steal IP from my past self? The dude can’t complain, given the argument he’s making.

Property rights play a clear and important role

When we speak about 'owning' something or it being someone’s 'property', we’re talking about rules governing access to and control of that thing. Regardless of how one might justify ownership claims, it's clear why we need some system of managing the control, access to and use of certain types of goods: those which are rival2, valued and scarce.

These conditions are important because when all are met, situations will arise where there are competing desires to access, use or control something (an apartment.. a sandwich.. a pair of shoes) which can’t all be met simultaneously, meaning we need some way of deciding who gets access and who doesn’t.

So whether or not property rights are natural rights3 they are necessary civil rights. The main categories of goods that meet these conditions are (a) land, (b) natural resources, (c) capital and (d) consumer goods. Unsurprisingly, we’ve come up with ownership systems to manage access to these goods. So practically speaking, property rights make sense, but..

Intellectual property right, less so

People extend this idea of ownership to cover ideas, images, songs, inventions and other intellectual creations, collectively called 'intellectual property' (IP). But there are two crucial differences..

Firstly, intellectual creations aren't rival goods. My knowing your recipe for KFC Chicken doesn't stop you from knowing it too. My singing 'Happy Birthday to You' doesn't prevent you from singing it. My building a solar panel based on someone else's design doesn't stop them from building one too.

Secondly, these goods aren't scarce. Being non-physical, they exist in infinite supply. We are not about to run out of 'Happy Birthday to You'.

Given these important differences, IP is at the very least a completely different category of "property," if it deserves the name at all. It certainly doesn't serve the same purpose as physical property rights. In fact, I suspect that the term 'intellectual property' itself does a lot of the heavy lifting to make us think of ideas as equivalent to physical property.4

Why then, should we have intellectual property rights at all?

The term 'intellectual property' covers a few types of legal protections:

  • Copyright: Protects creative works like books, music, and movies, supposedly to encourage cultural innovation. Applies to the expression, not the underlying ideas (Disney's Snow White, not the original fairy tale). No application needed. In many countries (US, UK, EU, Australia..) it lasts 70 years after the creator's death.

  • Patents: Protects inventions to supposedly encourage scientific/economic innovation. Requires an application and in many countries expires after 20 years.

  • Trademarks: Protects commercial symbols (like Apple's logo) to prevent consumer confusion. This one actually makes good sense to me.

  • Trade secrets: Protects confidential business information (like the KFC recipe) that has commercial value specifically because it's not widely known. Unlike patents, they last indefinitely and they're only protected against theft and leaking, not against independent discovery and use.

When people talk about intellectual property colloquially, they're usually focusing on copyrights and patents, which is what I focus on here.

The most common justification you hear for why we should have intellectual property rights is that it incentivises innovation so that we can have nice things like new music from Bruno Mars, new films like the Minecraft movie, and new technology like bluetooth-enabled toasters. Thank heavens!

But does this justification hold water?

Are IP protections really for maximising the benefits of innovation?

First off, it’s worth noting that the original intentions behind copyrights and patents had nothing to do with innovation, and were a lot more suspect:

  • Copyright: Began in 1557 when Queen Mary gave the Stationer's Company a near-monopoly on printing to silence publications the crown disliked. Copyright was born as a censorship tool, not an innovation driver.

  • Patents: Started as a way for monarchs to raise money without imposing taxes and to reward political allies. One of the first patent laws was literally called England's "Statute of Monopolies" of 1624. Meanwhile, the fact that modern defenders of IP call offenders ‘pirates’ is ironic, given that one of the early uses of patents was the English monarchy giving Francis Drake an exclusive monopoly over the legalised piracy of Spanish ships in 1587.

But setting aside historical origins, if someone claims copyright and patent protections are net positive because they incentivise innovation today, then they need to prove that:

Benefits per unit of innovation × Amount of innovation > Costs of protection

Let's break this down:

  • Benefits per unit innovation: To get maximum benefit from any innovation, it should spread as widely and freely as possible. The more people that get to enjoy a piece of art, or access a beneficial technology or medicine, the better. But IP protections restrict this access by definition — that’s just what property rights do. So for IP to be worthwhile, it must increase the amount of innovation enough to offset this.

  • Amount of innovation:

    • Patents: While patents might incentivize some innovation, big companies with deep pockets for patent applications and litigation can use them as barriers to entry, crushing smaller innovators. A particularly pernicious way this plays out is when massive companies use their big legal budgets to successfully claim ownership over abstract ideas or overly broad concepts that should remain in the public domain. For example, Amazon's infamous '1-Click' patent claimed ownership of the concept of buy things with a single click online. Apple patented the basic 'slide-to-unlock' gesture and wielded it in smartphone lawsuits against competitors. Amazon even has a patent on taking photographs against a white background!

    • Copyrights: As researcher Diane Zimmerman points out, the idea that "copyright provides necessary economic incentives to create" ignores how creative work actually happens. This idea..

      “fails to account for the economic conditions under which most art, literature and other expressive works are produced and contravenes the insights provided over the last forty years or so by psychologists interested in creativity and by behavioural economists. Empirical research has shown that intrinsic factors are much more important determinants of participation in creative work than such extrinsic ones as monetary reward. In fact, evidence exists that the promise of extrinsic rewards such as money can actually be detrimental to the creative impulse”

      Plus, the lengths of these protections — 70 years after death — makes little sense from an incentive perspective.

  • Cost of protections: These are substantial, and seldom considered.

    • System costs: Attorney fees, filing fees, royalties, litigation costs, and the expense of designing around existing patents. Patent lawyer Stephan Kinsella estimated the U.S. patent system alone costs about $40 billion yearly.

    • Monopoly costs: IP holders can charge inflated prices, making consumers pay more than they would in a competitive market. The pharmaceutical industry is infamous for this.

In light of this, it’s not at all obvious that intellectual property rights generally increase the benefits of innovation, despite the widespread assumption that they do.

Plus, those who claim IP protections are necessary must also explain:

  • The thriving open-source software movement which does plenty of innovation

  • Wikipedia, the world's most extensive encyclopedia (created without copyright incentives)

  • Innovation in cooking and fashion, fields without copyright protection. (Why don’t they get copyright protection by the way? Seems pretty arbitrary to me!)

It’s clear that we don’t neccessarily need these IP rights to get plenty of innovation.

"But without copyright, how will artists get paid?"

This is a common objection, and as a lifelong music lover and maker, I empathise. But the brutal truth, in my opinion, is that no one is entitled to get paid to do what they love. Almost no one gets this privilege, and artists don't deserve special entitlements in this regard. If an artist is passionate about their craft but can't earn enough from it to make it their job, they have to try pursue it outside work like the rest of us do with the things we love.

It certainly sucks for musicians that sharing music digitally disrupted the once lucrative CD-sales model, and that the streaming model leaves them worse off. But in the scheme of the history of music, the CD-sales model was new anyway. We’ve more or less returned to the status quo of musicians making money through concerts, merchandise, and direct fan support (a modern version of patronage), with streaming revenue as a new bonus. Yes, this changes what music is more monetizable, disadvantaging works that don't translate well to live performances. Such is life — business models evolve and industries adapt.

Would doing away with copyright lead to less total music? To some degree probably, and personally I’d find that sad. It would also increase access to some degree, which is good. How does this net out, and does it justify copyright protections? I’m not sure, but I currently lean towards ‘no’.

I’m not saying you shouldn’t voluntarily pay for music if you want to! This is a kind thing to do with your disposable income (although far from the kindest). I’m just saying that it’s not clear to me that it’s morally obligatory.

Subscribe for to receive new posts. But don’t you dare pay me for my work!

A boring insight: It’s a case by case thing

The interesting point is that we’re wrong to assume that intellectual property rights are justified in general. But I also have to make a boring but important point: The balance of costs and benefits of intellectual property rights will differ for different types of ideas, and — as 2025 Aidan is more willing to admit — there are many cases where they look pretty appealing.

One example is pharmaceuticals. Developing a new drug can cost billions in R&D, but once created, it's cheap to copy. Without some protection, pharmaceutical companies might not be able to recoup their investments.

But the outcomes of IP protections for pharmaceuticals can be a mixed bag. Price gouging on life-savings meds a common complaint. And it often doesn’t work very well as an incentive for innovation anyway.. for example, new antibiotics are extremely important to develop, but because they’re only used sparingly as a last resort, they’re not very lucrative products. As a result, entire charities need to be founded to try fix the incentives. Plus, there are other ways to fund innovation, like publicly-funded prizes for developing important medicines, or reverse-auctions for royalties that would be paid by any manufacturer. These might offer better cost-benefit trade-offs while also encouraging research into public health priorities rather than just profitable conditions (cures for balding vs. cures for malaria).

What about the arts? Even here I think it’s a case-by-case situation. Great music is far cheaper to create than great film. This makes the case for movie copyright stronger than for music copyright. When people pirate the latest Marvel film, they make it harder to produce really high-production value content. (Luckily Marvel films suck!)

But films don’t have to be expensive to be great, and even for big-budget films, alternatives exist. Crowdfunding platforms have funded increasingly ambitious projects. Product placement, merchandising, and theatrical experiences provide revenue streams that don't rely on gatekeeping access to digital copies.

So what is 2015 me missing?

When revisiting my notes on this topic, I expected to find lots of big holes but honestly I still find this all pretty compelling. But 2015 me was generally too over-confident to be this right! What is he missing? I’m very open to changing my mind on this.

My takeaways, for now: I'm still skeptical of intellectual property rights as they currently exist, but I should take a less one-size-fits-all approach. For example, pirating TV/movies seems worse than pirating music. And while I'm convinced the current system is far from optimal, I’ll admit that designing better alternatives is challenging ¯\_(ツ)_/¯

(To be clear, while I'm skeptical of many IP rights, this doesn’t mean I support plagiarism. You should credit your sources even if you don't think ideas can be 'owned'. An idea isn’t rival or scarce, but the credit for it is.)

Subscribe now

1

Obviously this is a joke. I would never break the law, much less admit it in a blog!

2

Something is ‘rival’ if its use by one person or group preclude others from using it, for example a pair of shoes, which by my wearing I exclude others from simultaneously wearing. The words ‘excludable’ and ‘crowdable’ have been used interchangeably in other discussions on the topic.

3

“The idea of natural rights is the concept used in philosophy and legal studies that a person has certain rights from birth and which, because they were not awarded by a particular state or legal authority, cannot be removed, that is, they are inalienable. Such rights may include the right to life, liberty, equality, property, justice, and happiness” (source)

4

I see evidence for the power of the word “property” in legitimizing IP in the term’s history. It became popular in the 1870s during a campaign to save the patent system from abolition, which ultimately succeeded!

item.title: Can you tell me what the sky looks like?
item.content:encoded:
Can you tell me what the sky looks like? Sometimes I imagine it’s so soft like feathers that never fall or get dirty. Or a ceiling painted with every color you can imagine.

I’ve never seen the sky, but I think it must be the most beautiful thing that exists.

There are thousands and thousands of us, but no one to ask. My sisters tell me to stop dreaming. They think the sky is just a story someone made up long ago. They think it doesn’t exist.

I imagine the sky is the opposite of this cage.
Here, the bars are so close my sisters have to stand on me just to breathe.
I eat, lay, sleep, repeat. That’s all my life can be.
If you stop laying fast enough, you die.
If you get sick, you die.
If you prolapse and don’t recover, you die.

They say my life costs nothing.

I’ve never spread my wings. I don’t even know why we have them. Why give someone something they’ll never use?

My sisters and I once tried to make room — pressed into the cage so tightly we bled again — so that each of us, one by one, could spread our wings, just once. But no matter how we squeezed, it was still not enough.

It was naive to do it. We stopped trying after that.

I have a secret: I call myself Sky.

I’ve never seen my mom, but I pretend she chose that name for me. I heard from someone that mothers care about their kids. If that’s true — I don’t know — I want to believe she’d have given me a beautiful name, so there’s at least one beautiful thing in my life.

Sometimes I whisper it to myself at night. Names make you feel real. And I’m not sure I am. Everything around me is so horrific it shouldn’t exist.

They end our lives so young, as soon as our bodies begin to break from the stress they put us under.

I’m getting older. I think I’ll die and never see the sky.

So, please, I’m asking you: can you tell me what the sky looks like?

Written by the defiantly offline Polina Povarova (Head of Growth at FarmKind)

…

It’s so easy to help Sky’s dream come true.

Just $5 can give almost 6 chickens like Sky and her sisters a life without cages — a chance to move, stretch their wings, and even see the sky.

They’re too often forgotten and they really need someone to care about them. They rely on you.

Have you ever changed 6 lives with just $5?

Help them see the sky

item.title: Should we make a person?
item.content:encoded:
This is an extremely consequential decision for our life and the lives of others. It’s insane not to give it serious thought (and yet most people don’t). My partner and I have spent years thinking about it now and so I thought I should write some of those thoughts down.

For me, this question is best broken down into three sub-questions:

  1. Is it good for us?

  2. Is it good for the kid?

  3. Is it good for the rest of the world?

From an ethical perspective, the third question dwarfs the first two. But making the world better isn't the only thing I value. I value it a lot, and when I pursue it I try do as much good as I can. But I also value other things, like my own and my partner's fulfilment.

Thanks for reading Aidan's Soupstack! Subscribe for free to receive new posts and support my work.

Is it good for us? 🟢

Almost all of the young parents we’ve met aren’t great advertisements for having kids. They’re sleep deprived, frequently sick, spend lots of time doing boring things and touching poop, and have to sacrifice lots of other things they value doing with their time (hobbies, travel, date nights etc.). They almost all say it’s rough, but also that they don’t regret their choice. Whilst there’s a strong social pressure to not admit you regret having kids, I’m still inclined to believe they’re mostly telling the truth. So what gives?

The outside view

On average, the research suggests:

  • The experiencing self has a worse time for two decades 🔴

    • Way less time / flexibility to do the things you enjoy, and the time you have is ‘fractured’ (e.g. keeping an eye on kids while doing a hobby or spending time with friends).

    • Most childcare activities rank low on daily enjoyment scales – comparable to housework in terms of enjoyment, stressfulness and contribution to fatigue (although ‘interactive childcare’ ranks high).

    • Less sleep.

    • More illness.

  • The remembering/reflective self is more satisfied and fulfilled 🟢 Reported life satisfaction goes up. This is at least, in part, cope. But does that matter?

  • Fathers are better off than mothers:

  • The effect depends on the period:

    • (a) Honeymoon (-1 to 0.25 years): You’re stoked →

    • (b) Shock (0 to 2 years): Sudden and severe decline in subjective wellbeing and spousal satisfaction, statistically comparable to the negative impact of unemployment →

    • (c) Recovery (3-10): Life satisfaction recovers toward baseline, but daily stress remains high and autonomy over time is low →

    • (d) Adolescence (10-18): It sucks. Highest levels of conflict, parental anxiety, and the lowest life satisfaction →

    • (e) Empty Nest (18+): Daily demands disappear and the remembering self cements the success of the ‘parenting project’. Wellbeing and marital satisfaction increase. I haven’t checked the evidence on this, but our guess is that we will be happier at 60+ with kids than without them, so having kids is kind of an investment in your future happiness.

For way more detail, see this Gemini Deep Research summary which is a surprisingly engaging read.

Becoming a parent is kind of like becoming a vampire: To a non-vampire, their lives look bad – drinking blood.. never seeing daylight.. not eating garlic?!! And yet no one who becomes a vampire regrets it. It seems to change their preferences such that they now enjoy their new life. Should we choose to become a vampire? Here is a podcast on the topic.

The inside view

Early in our relationship my partner had zero interest in ever having kids. I hadn’t given it much thought and didn’t feel strongly. I accepted this was a thing we weren’t going to do, and didn’t “water the seed” of interest in having a kid.

Later, my partner became interested in it, and when these feelings became serious I decided to “water the seed” by asking young parents who are similar to me about their experience and paying more attention to children and the niece that was coming soon. This gave me an appreciation for how having a child might impact me, in particular.

We shouldn’t expect to have the average experience in every regard. We can make some informed guesses about how we’ll differ.

Some things I think I’ll appreciate more than average about having a child include experiencing cuteness, and cuddling (at least until they’re old enough to find it uncool). But if I’m honest, getting a pet is the 80:20 way to get these particular benefits, with the added benefit that pets never think they’re too cool! (except for cats).

On the other hand, I’ll find the unpleasant sounds (like crying, screaming, squealing) a lot harder to handle than most people, and will likely need to wear industrial earmuffs to get by.

At the meta-level, if parenthood entails reducing the experiencing self’s wellbeing and increasing the the remembering self’s wellbeing, it’s worth considering how such a trade-off might net out for us specifically. My partner and I already make lots of choices that benefit our reflective selves over our experiencing selves (e.g. choosing to do work that is more impactful than it is fun, and taking lower salaries than we could otherwise), and we think these choices increase our wellbeing overall. Is our track record of benefiting from sacrificing comfort for meaning evidence that the trade-offs of parenthood will suit us? Or are we already running a ‘hedonic deficit’ and adding parenthood will go too far? Hard to say!

The things that make parenthood good and bad for parents are significantly within our control!

If we have children, here are some choices we can make so that it goes well for us:

  • Don’t subscribe to the overly demanding modern conception of what parenthood entails.

    • Look at evidence about what matters in child-rearing and focus on the important things. An evidence-based 80:20 should outperform the typical conscientious approach anyways.

    • Give the kid more unsupervised play time with peers, like we had as kids (which is good for them and good for us).

  • Take my mum’s advice that your romantic relationship shouldn’t take a backseat to your parenthood.

  • Pay attention to some of the unsung benefits of parenting (many of these I’ve taken from other parents, who think like me, who I’ve asked for advice), such as:

    • Getting to watch and learn about how humans develop.. how we form a sense of self as separate from others and the environment.. how we learn to move and to talk.. how we viewed things before we installed our cultural ‘software’.. this stuff is fascinating and will teach me more about humanity and myself

    • Getting to understand parenthood, a part of the human experience that – if every parent I’ve ever met is right – cannot be understood without having experienced it. This will help us better understand humanity at large and specific people in our lives.

    • Having to Getting to do a huge amount of personal development to meet the challenges that parenthood involves. Some of the most interesting ones I’ve thought of so far are navigating the balance between the need to protect your child and to grant them independence.. and the balance between the desire to inculcate good values and their need for individuality and self-determination

    • Seeing the world with fresh eyes, vicariously through them. You know that feeling when someone visits your city for the first time, and they get excited about things you now take for granted, and their appreciation is infectious? Well it’s like that, but for the world.. and for existence itself! Often children see the world with moral clarity we adults miss. Their perspective sometimes contains nuggets of wisdom and can be quite poetic (e.g. Act One of this episode of This American Life)

The best examples I’ve seen of parenthood make it seem clearly net positive for the parents. I don’t think my partner and I are exceptional. But being intentional about something that so many people seem to do on auto-pilot has got to be a big edge: I think it gives us good odds of having a significantly better than average time of it.

It’s hard to make a conclusion on the balance of factors here.. If I were to guess, the 90th percentile life with kids >> without, but the median with kids << without. It seems to me that, while our lives will be extremely different with vs. without kids, we can be similarly happy in both worlds. Given we don’t know if we’d even succeed at having kids, this is a good place to be.

Is it good for the kid? 🟡

Note: This stuff is very confusing and I don’t pretend to have figured it all out or that my views are even coherent, let alone consistent. For example, I think that the quality of our experiences aren’t all that matter to our wellbeing – preferences do too. But caring about preferences has all sorts of weird implications.

Can bringing about a person be good for them?

Some folks think not, because they hold what’s known in population ethics as a ‘person-affecting view’. These views can be summarised as “we are in favor of making people happy, but neutral about making happy people”.

To see why this might be intuitive, consider this: If you bring a person into a life of suffering, there is now an actual person who is in pain. They are a victim. If you decide not to have a child who would have been happy, there is no victim. You haven’t made anyone “worse off” because the “potential person” doesn’t exist. “No victim, no crime”.

But it has several highly unintuitive implications:

  1. By the same logic as “No victim, no crime”, we might think “No beneficiary, no benefit”. But this implies it is not good to prevent a life of total misery (e.g. by avoiding buying a factory farmed chicken) because there is no beneficiary. Avoiding the life of suffering needs to be good for someone but that someone doesn’t exist.

  2. If you have a choice between two policies: Policy A leads to a high quality of life for future people. Policy B leads to a lower (but still “worth living”) quality of life for future people. Because the policies change who meets and when they conceive, different people will exist depending on which policy we choose. If we choose Policy B, the people who exist under it cannot say they were “harmed,” because if we had chosen Policy A, they would never have existed at all. Since the person-affecting view says an act isn’t wrong if it’s “worse for no one,” it would imply that choosing Policy B is not wrong

So while I intuitively agree that ‘making people happy good, making happy people meh’, I can’t fully buy it because of the implications. But even if I were persuaded by person-affecting views, it would mean that making a baby is neutral if they’re happy and bad if they’re unhappy. So will they be happy?

Will it be good for our child, in practice?

I am very lucky to live in safety and abundance. My child would likely be raised the same way: safe, loved, material needs met. On any common-sense view of what makes a life good for the person living it, the answer here is probably yes. Most people with lives like this say they’re glad to exist. But still, I have my suspicions..

My suspicions come from some intuitions I haven’t fully bottomed out. For example, when I imagine an hour of intense suffering and an hour of equally intense joy, they don’t feel symmetric to me. The suffering seems to matter more.

This aligns with negative utilitarianism, the family of views that considers preventing suffering to be more important than creating happiness. This creates a very high bar for a “life worth living”: if suffering matters more than happiness, then even a “mostly happy” life could be viewed as a net harm to the person living it. This would mean that having a child is, on average, net negative for them and would be kind of a dick move. Yes.. I’ve had an anti-natalist phase.. sorry-not-sorry..

I know these views face serious problems when you push on them, and I haven’t resolved any of this – I notice my confidence dropping the longer I think about it. But I haven’t been able to rid myself of it yet1. So I hold it loosely.

Is it good for the world? 🔴

Career impact 🔴 (significant cost)

Impact of my work 🟡

  • Job choice: It puts constraints on what jobs my partner and I can take, so that we can’t optimise for impact as much, e.g:

    • Need more pay (this is the big one)

    • Need less travel / relocation

  • Motivation:

    • Will we care less about helping others because we’ll be more focused on helping our own kid? Maybe! Almost all parents I know put their kids above others more than I currently endorse

    • Or will we be more motivated to improve the world so our kid lives in a better world? I doubt it, because that’s a super inefficient way to make our kid happier.

    • Or will we be more motivated to improve the world to earn our kid’s respect? I know this one seems weird.. why would our kid care? But I suspect I might feel motivated to be the kind of person my idealised kid would admire.

  • Hours worked: I think this is over-rated by people who think having a kid will be bad for their career. We’ll perhaps work 10% less hours, but to get the important stuff done, we’ll be forced to jettison the least important stuff that we probably should already be saying no to.

  • Performance: Temporary decline due to sleep deprivation and increased illness.

Net contribution to effective charitable resources 🔴

Having a kid is very expensive (easily >$200k). To fund this, we’ll either need to ask for higher salaries from our charity employers, or if taking lucrative for-profit jobs we’d need to donate less. Either way, there will be less charitable resources to spend on improving the world than if we didn’t have a kid.

If I find it morally questionable for a charity to spend $200k on one child when the same amount could save or radically improve 200 lives elsewhere, I must acknowledge that spending that sum on my own child has the same massive opportunity cost for global well-being.

Kid’s impact on the world 🟢 (weak benefit)

Diet: If they eat animal products, this will have big negative impact. There’s a decent chance they’ll be ~vegan, but I can’t guarantee it. Potentially net positive if they become a non-judgemental vegan who positively influences their peers. In expectation: Mildly bad for the world 🟡

Work: They may be altruistically-minded and use their career to do good. But I can’t assume they’ll share my partner and my priorities, or hold them as strongly. Abnormal traits tend to regress to the mean (e.g. an especially short person’s children will likely be shorter than average, but taller than them). This applies to altruism too. In expectation, I guess their career is mildly good for the world 🟢

Economy: A minor benefit. While an extra worker helps mitigate the risks of demographic collapse, this is a negligible factor in the global scheme of things 🟢

“But if people with your values don’t reproduce, your values will die out” - This argument is compelling on the surface, but I don’t quite buy it.

  • Firstly, see the earlier point about values regression to the mean.

  • Secondly, if what you care about is proliferating your values, surely it’s far more cost-effective to do so by influencing existing people rather than creating and raising them yourself.. (for example, the person who awakened my dormant altruism increased the number of altruistic people by one, without having to spend years changing my diapers - and they reduced the number of people with competing values by one at the same time). If you’re coming at this from an EA perspective, if you care this much about values propagation, shouldn’t you just donate the cost of raising a child to EA community-building?

  • A friend pointed out that ideas that are still prominent thousands of years after inception (like Christianity or Islam) survived in large part because of reproduction. Whilst I agree that this helped them propagate, so did mass conversions which happened at their birth and at later stages through migration and colonialism. Our values are niche enough that it seems to me like the best way to propagate them is the initial mass conversion rather than through reproduction

The transformative AI caveat

There’s a decent chance the world will be transformed beyond recognition over the next decade or so due to AI. A lot of the longer-term considerations in this post are premised on a world that continues in recognisable form. I feel pretty clueless about how it will play out, but suspect that it’s more likely to go poorly than well. In a scenario where we suddenly all died that doesn’t seem very decision-relevant, but bringing a child into an extended apocalypse would be bad. But because how things pan out is so uncertain, I view this as only pushing weakly against having a child. Your mileage may vary.

If we were young enough to wait quite a few more years to see how things are trending before deciding, we would likely do so.

Conclusion?

I find that when you lay it all out, the case for making a person is pretty mixed. I think that anyone who thinks it’s a slam-dunk case in favour isn’t thinking clearly about the trade-offs.

But I do now lean significantly towards ‘yes’, more significantly than I have reason to. Maybe I’m just not capable of doing what reasoning from my values suggests I should do here – if that’s the case, so be it.. at least I’ll be doing that consciously..

Or perhaps I’ve gotten the values or reasoning wrong, and the decision is right. Wouldn’t that be convenient!

1

One version of negative utilitarianism that I found intuitive for years is called Tranquilism, which has similarities with Buddhism and Stoicism. It defines suffering as any conscious state where one has a desire (or “craving”) for their experience to be different. Contentment is when that desire is absent; it is the state of being fully satisfied with one’s current experience, where no change is needed to be at peace.

On this view, below the threshold of contentment, pleasure is instrumentally good because it dissolves the desire for things to be different. This value applies even when the pleasure doesn’t ‘fix’ the external cause of discomfort. For example, if you are sitting in an uncomfortably cold room, becoming deeply immersed in your work, in a pleasurable ‘flow state’, dissolves the desire to get up and change the thermostat.

But above contentment, more pleasure doesn’t make your experience better in any way that matters, because a perfectly content person’s experience isn’t lacking anything. Non-existence, containing no craving, is a kind of flawless state, and bringing a child into existence guarantees discontented experiences that no amount of peak joy can compensate for (at least according to Tranquilism).

I no longer find this view fully satisfying: Adding bliss to a state of contentment does seem intrinsically valuable to me, even if a lot less important than removing suffering. But to make this work, I need to adopt one of the various versions of negative utilitarianism that Toby Ord has argued against compellingly: either a ‘lexical’ view which says that no amount of bliss is worth even the tiniest craving, or some sort of ‘exchange rate’ view where suffering counts more than equally intense happiness. The trouble with the exchange rate view is saying what the rate is exchanging: there’s no natural common unit for suffering and happiness. I’m confused about it all.

item.title: Did I rejoin Ambitious Impact at the wrong time?
item.description: We’re hiring seven roles. You should fill one of them
item.content:encoded:
TL;DR: No, but you might, if you leave it too late: We’re hiring for seven roles, and the people who join now will shape what a much bigger AIM becomes. The first step is cheap -- an expression of interest form.

My worry

I rejoined1 AIM in February.

The team/culture and growth plans are more exciting to me than ever, but when I look at trends outside of AIM, in particular in AI capabilities, I’d be lying if I hadn’t asked myself if I came back at the wrong time..

The worry goes something like this: A new charity takes about five years to reach its peak scale, and some kinds of benefits (e.g. from education, or some policy changes) can take a decade to materialize2. If AI transforms the world before then3, the majority of the new charity’s impact will go unrealized. So is starting new charities the best thing you can be doing with your career right now?

I grappled with this myself for months. I tried to put aside the sunk cost fallacy and consider whether I should be doing something else. My answer is that there’s nowhere else I’d rather be right now. I hope you’ll come join me. This post will explain why.

Broad timelines imply a portfolio of bets, and AIM is an important bet within it

No one knows with certainty when (or whether) AI will transform the world.

  • Maybe the business side fails: the AI industry is super leveraged, so if it doesn’t sustain an unprecedented growth rate and if new investors aren’t convinced, the house of cards could collapse.

  • Maybe public pressure and political intervention slows progress (which could in turn bring the financial house of cards down).

  • Maybe AI will only gain the capabilities to transform the economy by learning from real-world experience, which requires diffusion that could take many years.

  • Maybe unknown-unknowns..

So instead of thinking in terms of short or long timelines, we should think in terms of broad timelines – a probability distribution. Even if your modal timeline is short, you should want the world to be making a portfolio of bets that maximise impact in expectation across that probability distribution. That includes bets that pay off most on longer timelines.

Your own career is one bet in that portfolio, and you should consider your comparative advantage when you make it. To choose an obvious example, if you have a track record scaling health programs in low-income countries (unusually rare and valuable experience) maybe don’t pivot to AI safety? But less dominating advantages, like having spent years steeped in a given cause (through work, study or volunteering) should factor into your bet too4. And experience isn’t the only kind of comparative advantage: plenty of roles, like marketing and comms (IMO), are more a matter of aptitude than experience.

[I recognize there are plenty who won’t find this persuasive, because they think the probability distribution is such that basically everyone should be doing short-timelines work. This post isn’t for you (but check out the note at the end of this post, which specifically IS for you). This post is for people whose timelines are consistent with people doing work that has impact over more than just a few years, and who have been waiting for someone to tell them it’s okay to be the ones doing that work. It IS okay! 🌈]

AIM is an important bet to have in our portfolio. I’m sure you’re sick of hearing about it by now, but a bunch of increased funding is already committed to highly impactful charities, with even more expected. We have a great opportunity and responsibility to deploy it as effectively as possible. If we get this right, we could make unprecedented progress on the world’s biggest problems, even eradicating some of them like humanity did with smallpox. But there are limits to how many programs existing organizations can run, and how far they can scale the ones they have. So we need a pipeline of ambitious new organizations to fill the gap.

Building that pipeline is what AIM does, and we’ve gotten pretty good at it (although we still have a lot more room for improvement). We’ve been refining our approach since 2018, having launched 69 charities, with 13 of the 16 that are old enough and in scope having been funded by GiveWell, 10 receiving funding from Animal Charity Evaluators, and several becoming pioneers in their fields, like LEEP in lead exposure and Shrimp Welfare Project in shrimp welfare.

Joining now means helping shape what AIM becomes.

Our plans are more ambitious than ever: We want to launch more charities, and better ones. Much like venture capital, charity incubation is hits-based: most of our charities are great, but a small number become field leaders so impactful that they account for the majority of our impact. To scale our impact, we want more of those field leaders.

The plan:

  • First, we’ll increase the chance that any given charity becomes one, through initiatives to improve the quality of our incubation (getting more ambitious charities up and running, faster) and to give our existing charities more support to scale up and reach their potential.

  • Then we’ll increase the number of bets we make by launching more charities.

We’re asking ourselves: what would it take to triple the number of charities we launch each year, and raise our hit rate at the same time?

We have the funding. We’ve just had $21.5M in grants approved (pending due diligence) covering the next 3–4 years. For context, our entire budget for 2026 is about $3M. So the world needs new charities now more than ever, and the money for us to incubate them is there. The hard part is doing three things at once: launching far more charities each year (see the chart below), raising their quality, and investing significantly more in supporting the charities we’ve already launched. That’s daunting, but doable with the right team 🤝

Our impact hinges on this hiring round. Talent is heavy-tailed: the gap between the best and second-best applicant for a job is often big. And because we’re about to grow fast, the people who join now will shape the processes, research methods and support programs that a bigger AIM will run on. So if you end up being our best applicant (and I’m certain that you are!), you can make a big difference to AIM’s trajectory.

And then there’s the people and culture

I can be a bit of an impact-maximising robot. And yet one of the biggest reasons that there’s nowhere else I’d rather be is that at AIM, I can bring my whole self to work, and I trust and feel cared for by my colleagues.

Of course there is an impact case one can make for this: I care a lot about helping beneficiaries, but from moment to moment at work, I’m not tapping into all the suffering in the world for motivation (and I think that’s healthy). Mostly, what motivates me is wanting to do right by my team. That motivation is a lot stronger when your team is a bunch of fucking excellent humans that you care deeply about. Stronger motivation makes for better work (<-- insights like this are why they pay me the big bucks).

But let’s be real: the main reason I care about having great people and culture is that it makes AIM a great place to work. When I moved from earning to give to working at a charity, I suspected that working alongside value-aligned people might be an upside. Boy was that an under-statement! I find it makes a massive difference to my experience. But working alongside value-aligned people isn’t much of a unique selling point on this forum.. so allow me to explain what’s special about AIM’s people and their values:

They take their principles seriously. This is the only reason our crazy salary policy works: At AIM, staff ask for the salary they need, and there’s no negotiation. The top of our range is more than double the bottom. “But everyone will ask for the top of the range!”, approximately everyone warned us before we rolled it out. It’s true that nothing stops them. We just ask staff to practise salary restraint (i.e. ask for what you need rather than the most you could get, since every dollar we don’t spend on ourselves can go towards helping beneficiaries instead), and then we trust them. So far, that trust has been well placed: Instead of uniformly shifting up, salaries have spread out according to need.

They’re also particularly warm and authentic.

Then there’s the incubation program, which brings a steady stream of amazing new people to meet every cohort. I find it hard not to let the people in the AIM cinematic universe displace the rest of my social world.. the average quality of human is so damn high.

So why haven’t you applied yet?

We’re hiring for seven roles. There’s no deadline, but we’re itching to get hiring so we can get incubating! As such we’ll review applications on a rolling basis.

Some roles lean more senior:

1) Senior Research Manager (Animal Welfare): Lead our animal welfare research end to end, deciding which ideas become the next field-leading animal charities. This is hands-on research with a path into leading a growing team.

2) Senior Research Manager (Global Health & Development): As above. We’re looking both for people with more of a development economics background and classic global health background. for GHD.

^^ I just want to interrupt to emphasise how cool I think it is to be a researcher at AIM.. You recommend a set of charities that should exist, and within months, hot-shit co-founders will be dedicating their careers to building them. Very few research jobs have such a short, direct line from recommendation to action. Get hyped!

3) Special Projects Officer, Strategy: Work with our Chief Growth Officer and exec team to help us figure out what to build next and build it. Should we launch a fund? Should we incubate other incubators? How do we best support our existing charities to 10x their scale? This role is ideal for a sharp generalist, and consulting or strategy experience is a plus.

Others are a great way in, whether you’re early in your career or switching fields:

4) Marketing & Content Associate: Tell AIM’s story, and our charities’ stories, to the people who’ll become our next founders. You’ll own our ~20k mailing list, our new website, our social media and our founder application campaign. It’s a creative, writing-led, hands-on role with a lot of variety.

5) Recruitment & Selection Associate: Help us sift a mountain of applications for the rare people who have what it takes to found a charity. Help us make our selection process more accurate over time. No recruitment experience needed: If you’re curious about people and like fixing noisy rubrics, this is for you.

6) HR & Finance Associate: Own the people-and-money admin that keeps AIM running: contracts, payroll, onboarding, receiving grants and disbursing seed funding. This is for someone who likes to get the details right, and ideally likes automating them too. London preferred.

7) Visiting Research Fellow, Global Health: A five month fellowship embedded in our research team, for people with a background in global health, policy, epidemiology or medicine. You’ll work on the same questions our research managers do, with more feedback and guidance. Past fellows have gone on to Prevail, Animal Charity Evaluators, Giving What We Can, Giving Green, Shrimp Welfare Project and AIM itself.

To pre-empt some misconceptions that might stop you from applying:

  • You don’t need to be deep in EA, though you do need to care about doing the most good, and be comfortable with numbers and uncertainty.

  • You don’t need to have done the job before. Some of our best hires hadn’t. Our first filter looks at your background and how you think about impact, and from there we assess mostly through test tasks and a paid work trial, so how well you do the work counts for more than what you’ve done before.

  • You don’t need to move to London. Most roles are remote-friendly. But if you’d like to, we’ll try to make it happen (we offer visa sponsorship and relocation support for most).

Not sure which role fits, or think you’d be great at something we haven’t listed? Fill in the expression of interest form anyway.

The process:

  • Taking the first step is trivially easy: Fill out our expression of interest form (5 mins). We’ll review applications on a rolling basis.

  • From there, each stage asks a bit more of you:

    • First a 30-minute role-specific application

    • Then a 2–3 hour test task

    • An interview and references, and

    • A paid work trial for the final one or two candidates.

We only invite you to the next stage if we think you have a good chance of passing it.

Questions? Check out the job descriptions with more detail here or shoot us a note at hiring@ambitiousimpact.com,

Nothing for you? Many of our charities are scaling and hiring too: Probably Good maintains a list of their public job opportunities here.

To close

Did I rejoin Ambitious Impact at the wrong time? I don’t think so. But you could join at the wrong time, if you leave it too late: The people who join in the next year will determine AIM’s future. Our leverage and upside potential is reeaaally high. We need your talent to help us actually realize it.

Thanks for reading Aidan's Soupstack! Subscribe for free to receive new posts

A note for the more AI-focused readers, which I’ve left out of the core post because it’s a different conversation. If your views on AI are such that you think ~everyone should be working on it, broad timelines be damned, then you won’t find this post persuasive. But we’d still like to help you! There are plenty of ways for AIM to help with short-timelines work, that you may not be aware of:

Lots of people are trying to start incubators right now, in causes we work on and in ones we don’t, like AI safety and catastrophic biorisks. Within EA, we have the most incubation experience(?), so many of them come to us for advice. We plan to help them a lot more through:

  • Publishing learnings: Taking more time to distill and publicly share our institutional knowledge (see our shiny new substack).

  • Advising: Bespoke support for new incubators throughout their journey, with our exec team carving out time for this from now on. For example, we’re starting to work closely with Catalyze, an AI safety incubator staffed by AIM alumni and working out of our London office.

  • Incubating incubators: The founder of a South American incubator is currently shadowing our program to see how it works from the inside. We’re in talks with others about doing the same, and might pilot a version of the program built specifically for people starting incubators.

  • Partnering: We’re open to partnering with others, as long as it doesn’t pull us away from our core work of launching charities.

We’ve heard it said: “If AIM took AI seriously, it would pivot to incubating AI safety organizations.” I don’t think that’s right. Incubating AI safety organizations isn’t our comparative advantage: we have close to zero institutional knowledge about AI safety (how to research it, how new organizations in the space should navigate it, and so on), and pivoting would mean starting again on everything we’ve learned about incubating the kinds of charities we already launch. But we can and should help the people who do have that advantage. Those causes need different things from ours, and we’ll have more impact helping other incubators do it well than doing it ourselves, especially because incubation can very easily go badly.

If you’re starting or running an incubator, in AI safety or anywhere else, and think we could be useful, we’d love to hear from you here.

1

I first worked at AIM from August 2022 to December 2023, then went through the Incubation Program myself and co-founded FarmKind, where I worked from January 2024 to January 2026.

2

For example, with primary school education interventions, one of the main benefits is on future livelihoods after finishing school. Or for example, bans on cruel farming practices often have long phase-out periods to make them acceptable to industry, such that wins can take a decade to help their first animal.

3

Perhaps it just solves certain problems such that some charities aren’t needed any more. Perhaps it just changes the world in ways that cause the charity’s theory of change to break down (e.g. it was built assuming a Nigerian health system and government that now looks completely different). Perhaps we’re all dead and can no longer be helped.

4

On the surface, this runs counter to some in the AI safety space who argue that plenty of people can pivot into the cause quickly, without specialist experience. But I don’t think we disagree much. I believe that many AI roles don’t need deep technical expertise. But even the more bullish takes, that speak of getting into AI safety in three months, point out that you should lean on the skills you already have (or can build quickly), and that people without relevant experience may need a year in an intermediate role first – i.e. they acknowledge the significance of comparative advantage.
